content: An online survey form was developed using the Google Forms application and was made available in both English and French. The survey consisted of seven sections, which addressed topics such as the national hepatitis B program, the availability of health services for hepatitis B testing and treatment, and perspectives on potential updates to guidelines and recommendations for hepatitis B care. The survey link was distributed to national focal points and program managers for viral hepatitis from 52 countries. These individuals typically participate in monthly viral hepatitis ECHO webinars organized by the WHO Global Hepatitis Program. The data collected from the survey were cleaned and analyzed using Microsoft Excel and SPSS software. The findings were subsequently presented during the viral hepatitis ECHO webinar and the Guideline Development Group meeting, which focused on updating the WHO hepatitis B guidelines. Among the 52 countries contacted, 41 responses were received, representing 33 countries across six WHO regions, with multiple responses from some countries. The majority of responses were from the African Region. Specifically, 13 countries (32%) from the African Region participated, including Benin, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Congo, Gabon, Gambia, Ghana, Nigeria, Rwanda, South Africa, and Uganda. Other regions included the Region of the Americas (Brazil, Colombia, Peru; 7%), South-East Asia Region (Indonesia, Sri Lanka; 5%), European Region (Albania, Armenia, Georgia, Kyrgyzstan, Serbia, Spain, Uzbekistan; 17%), Eastern Mediterranean Region (Morocco, Pakistan; 5%), and Western Pacific Region (Cambodia, Kiribati, Lao People’s Democratic Republic, Malaysia, Philippines, Vanuatu; 15%). Regarding the background of the respondents, 51% were male, and 71% were employed at health ministries, with the remainder working at government hospitals or universities. Ninety percent of the respondents (37 individuals) were clinicians or medically qualified physicians. Among these, 65% had direct experience managing hepatitis B infections, and 71% dedicated more than three days per week to viral hepatitis program management. In terms of national hepatitis B programs, 71% of respondents reported the presence of national strategic plans for hepatitis B, 51% indicated the existence of national operational plans, and 76% noted the availability of national guidelines for hepatitis B. Additionally, 54% of respondents (22 out of 41) mentioned that their countries had government-funded programs for hepatitis B. Among these, 37% indicated that government-funded programs covered services for hepatitis B testing and diagnosis. Regarding the expansion of eligibility for hepatitis B treatment, 60% of respondents agreed or fully agreed with treating all HBsAg-positive cases with abnormal ALT levels above the upper limit of normal (Recommendation 5). Furthermore, 57% agreed or fully agreed with treating all HBsAg-positive cases with HBV DNA levels >2000 IU/mL for individuals aged >30 years, regardless of ALT levels (Recommendation 4). When asked about expanding eligibility for antiviral prophylaxis to prevent mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HBV, 71% of respondents fully agreed, 15% agreed, 7% were neutral, 2% disagreed, and 5% strongly disagreed with providing prophylaxis to all HBsAg-positive mothers when HBV DNA levels are unavailable. Regarding the inclusion of tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) or dual therapy with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) and lamivudine (3TC) for hepatitis B treatment, 73% of respondents agreed or fully agreed with using tenofovir or entecavir exclusively for hepatitis B treatment (Recommendation 1). Additionally, 66% agreed or fully agreed with using TAF (Recommendation 2), and 46% agreed or fully agreed with dual therapy TDF + 3TC (Recommendation 3). Concerning the simplification of hepatitis B service delivery, 93% of respondents noted that hepatitis B care is currently available at hospital-based clinics. More than three-quarters (78%) agreed or fully agreed with providing hepatitis B services at multiple hospital-based clinics, while 61% agreed or fully agreed with providing services at primary care clinics. Regarding the integration of hepatitis B services with pre-existing HIV clinics or noncommunicable disease clinics, 87% agreed or fully agreed with integrating hepatitis B services at HIV clinics, whereas only 51% agreed or fully agreed with integrating services at noncommunicable disease clinics. Finally, regarding the use of point-of-care HBV DNA viral load assays, 32% of respondents reported the availability or accessibility of laboratory-based HBV DNA testing in their countries, while only 14% noted the presence or accessibility of point-of-care testing. However, 54% of respondents agreed or fully agreed with utilizing HBV point-of-care DNA assays as an alternative to laboratory-based HBV DNA assays.
